name: Social Studies
fwnote: Codes are the Illinois Learning Standards for Social Science (adopted 2016, built on the C3 Framework), coded by strand (IS inquiry skills; CV civics; G geography; EC economics and EC.FL financial literacy; H history) and by grade (K-5), band (6-8, with LC/MdC/MC complexity levels) or 9-12; alignment was made by the course author and is not a certification.

1.bq: Who am I, who are my people, and how do rules help us live together?
std: SS.CV.2.K
Explain why rules are needed and what they are for at school and elsewhere
SS.CV.1.K
Describe what people in authority, like teachers and principals, do and are responsible for
SS.CV.2.1
Identify rules and explain how they work in different settings in and out of school
SS.CV.1.1
Explain that everyone in a community, not only leaders, has an important role
SS.IS.6.K-2
Use listening, consensus and voting to make decisions and act together in class
1.write: Pick one rule from your class or your home. Say what the rule is. Tell who could get hurt or feel sad without it. Tell why the rule is a good rule.
rooms: Me, my family, my class — cards, quiz and lab
Rules and fair choices — cards, quiz and lab

ch.t: Who I Am and Who I Live With
ch.bq: What makes me who I am, and who are the people I live with?
ch.talk: Who sits at your table? What story does your family tell again and again?

l.look: Which month has two names in it? What do Ana and Leo share?

l.t: Things I Like and Can Do
l.look: What does each drawing tell you about Ana? What would you put on your poster?
Whose family is the biggest? Whose is the smallest? Are they all families?
Count the ways people helped. Who helped Ana? Who did Ana help?
Why is the cake the same both years? What does your family do every year?
What is the same in the two photos? What is different?
What goes in the middle? What would be in the middle for you and a friend?
Find one thing that is different about each kid. What do they all share?

ch.t: Rules at School and at Home
ch.bq: Why do we have rules, and who gets to make them?
ch.talk: Why did Ms. Park let the kids make the rules instead of making them herself?

l.look: Who followed the rule? Who did not? What happened to each one?
Which way is fair? How do you know?
Why did Great-Grandma draw pictures? Which rule is a safety rule?

l.t: On the Bus and at the Pool
l.look: Which place has the most rules? Why might a pool need more rules than a library?
Which three rules won? Why did no gum lose?
What rule did Sam break? What three things did he do to make it right?
How does the talking stick help kids take turns? How does it help them listen?
What would happen at the corner without Ms. Lee? How is she a leader?

2.bq: How do people in a community help each other get what they need?
std: SS.CV.2.2
Describe how a community works together on shared tasks and assigns roles and responsibilities
Name some cultural and environmental features of your own community and compare them with other places
SS.EC.1.K
Explain that people make choices because they cannot have everything they want
SS.EC.1.1
Explain, with examples, that choosing one thing means giving something else up
SS.EC.2.1
Describe the skills and knowledge needed to produce particular goods and services
2.write: Leo has eleven dollars. Should he buy the ice cream cone now or save for the bike? Say what he should do. Tell what you read about needs, wants and saving. Tell why your choice is best.
rooms: Needs, wants and work — cards, quiz and lab

ch.bq: Who are the people in our community, and how do they help each other?
ch.talk: Rosa could not fix the swing alone. Who helped? What did each person do?
ch.story: The Day We Fixed the Swing

l.look: Who on Rosa's street is part of her community?
Which window shows a city? A town? The country? How do you know?
What did the nurse do to help Jamal?
Why does Ms. Kim walk in the snow? What would happen if she stayed home?
Pick one job. What happens to the town if no one does it?
Who uses the park the most? Who else uses it?
How did the class solve the trash problem? Could one kid do it alone in ten minutes?

ch.bq: How do people get the things they need and the things they want?
ch.talk: Leo had to choose: the cone now or the bike later. What would you choose? Why?

l.look: Find the four needs in the picture: food, water, shelter, clothes.
Which things in the bag are needs? Which are wants?
When did Leo sell the most cups? Why do you think so?
Which things they paid for were goods? Which were services?
What would you pick? What would you give up?
Does the jar go up or down each week? What is Leo doing?
Who traded? Who shared? How can you tell the difference?
Count the stops from field to bowl. Who did a job at each stop?
When is the farmer working? Is there a season with no work?

3.bq: How do maps and places help us understand where we live?
std: Make and read maps and other representations to find the way around a familiar place
Construct and interpret maps and graphics of familiar and unfamiliar places
Name cultural and environmental features of the local community and compare them with other places
SS.G.1.K
Explain how weather, climate and other environmental features affect how people live
With support, describe how human activities change the cultural and environmental features of places
3.write: Draw a map of the route from your classroom door to one place in your school. Then write: My map helps a new student because... Use the key, a direction word and one thing they pass.
rooms: Maps: where things are — cards, quiz and lab

ch.bq: How can a drawing help us find our way?
ch.talk: What did the class draw on the map? What did they leave out?

l.look: What would you draw if you made a map of your desk?
What is by the fence on this playground?
The neighborhood map has 40 squares. What might each square be?
Is the dog near the tree or far from it? How do you know?
Which direction is the park from Ana? Which direction is her house?

l.t: The Globe Is a Model of Earth
l.look: Are there more water parts or more land parts? What color will most of a globe be?
Which is bigger, Illinois or Chicago? How can you tell from the map?
Why might Mia's mom pick the longer route?

ch.t: Land, Water and Weather Where We Live
ch.bq: How does a place shape the people who live there, and how do people shape the place?
ch.talk: What did Nia see in the city that she did not see at the farm? What did she see at the farm that was not in the city?

l.look: Why do the kids sled on the hill and not on the field?
Which one could you walk around in a day? Which one could you never walk around?
What did people do to change the field from grass to corn?
Which month is hottest? Which is coldest? What would you wear in each?
Which backpack is for winter? Which is for summer? How do you know?
How did the people change the lot? What was there before?
Why does Town A have a net shop and Town B have a seed store?
What will the park look like next summer because of this day?

4.t: Then and Now, and Our Country
4.bq: How do we know about long ago, and what do we share as a country today?
std: SS.H.1.K
Compare how people lived in the past with how they live today
Summarize how the local community has changed over time
Explain how documents, objects, pictures and oral accounts can be used to study the past
SS.H.2.K
Explain what national holidays mean and the people and achievements they honor
Describe individuals and groups who brought about important historical change
SS.IS.6.K-2
Use listening, consensus and voting to make decisions and act together in class
4.write: Pick one thing that changed from long ago to today, like travel, phones or school. Draw or write: what it was like long ago, what it is like now, and one clue that shows it changed.
rooms: Then and now — cards, quiz and lab
Symbols and stories of our country — cards, quiz and lab

ch.bq: How do we know what life was like long ago?
ch.talk: What is one old thing in your home? What can it tell you about long ago?

l.look: Which picture is the past? Which is the present? Which is the future?
Name three clues in the photo that show it was taken long ago.
What changed? What stayed the same about the trip?
Which kitchen is from long ago? How can you tell?
What is one thing that changed? What is one thing that stayed the same?

l.t: A Town in One Hundred Years
l.look: When did Chicago have the fewest people? When did it have the most?
What changed in the two photos? What stayed the same?
Which event came first? Which came last? What might Maya add next?

ch.t: Symbols, Holidays and Being a Citizen
ch.bq: What do we share as a country, and what is my job in it?
ch.talk: Why was voting a fair way to pick the name? What else could the class have done?
ch.story: The Class Pet Gets a Name

l.look: What does each star stand for? What do the stripes stand for?
Find the words "liberty" and "justice." What do they mean?
Why do you think the eagle is on our money?
Why do you think she holds a light up high?
What did the people want? How did they ask for it?
Which parade is Independence Day? Which is Veterans Day? How do you know?
Who came to the house? How did it help them?
What should Nia do? What would a good citizen do?

5.bq: How have the land of Illinois and the people of Illinois shaped each other?
std: Construct and interpret maps of Illinois and the United States in various media
Analyze how the cultural and environmental features of Illinois places change over time
Locate major landforms and bodies of water on a map or other representation
Use artifacts and primary sources to investigate how people contributed to founding and developing Illinois
Explain probable causes and effects of events and developments in Illinois history
5.write: Make a claim: Which shaped Illinois more, its land or its people? Support your claim with at least three pieces of evidence from this unit, such as the glaciers and soil, the rivers and canals, the fire and rebuilding, or the Great Migration.
rooms: Communities and Illinois — cards, quiz and lab

ch.bq: How did the land of Illinois get the way it is, and how do people use it?
ch.talk: If you could see Illinois from an airplane two hundred years ago and today, what would look different? What might look the same?

l.look: Why might some borders be straight and others wiggle?
Which river is the longest? Which of these four rivers stays mostly inside Illinois?
Why is it so much cooler near the lake? What do you think happens on a cold winter day?
The highest and lowest points are less than 1,000 feet apart. What does that tell you about the shape of the state?
Dickens compared the prairie to the sea. What do a prairie and an ocean have in common?
How many times bigger is Chicago than the next biggest city? Which cities on this list are suburbs of Chicago?
Which region is each postcard from? What clue tells you?
What is happening? Why is an inside hallway with no windows the safest place?
Which natural resource does each person's job depend on? Which resource will still be there in a thousand years, and which could run out?
Corn and soybeans together cover about twenty million acres. About how many acres of wheat would fit in that space?
What problem did farmers have to solve before they could plant this land? How did they solve it?

ch.bq: How did Illinois change from a land of mound cities and prairie into the state we live in today?
ch.talk: Clara's family had a few minutes to grab what they could carry. What would you take? Why did people rebuild instead of leaving?

l.look: The mound was built one basket of dirt at a time. What does its size tell you about how many people worked on it and how they were organized?
This is the French side of the story. What might the Illinois villagers have been thinking as they watched these strangers arrive?
What did each side get from the trade? Why might a steel knife be worth a lot to someone who has never had one?
Between which two dates did the state grow the most? What do you think brought so many people?
Count how many times the wheat changed boats. Why was this still cheaper than carrying it by wagon?
Why did the grain elevator, hotel and store all cluster near the tracks? What would happen to this town if the trains stopped coming?
In which twenty-year stretch did the city grow the most? What happened in those years to bring so many people?
Why is a survivor's account useful to historians? What might a survivor remember wrong or leave out?
What pulled people to Chicago? What pushed them out of the South? What did they give up?
How are these three lives connected? What does each depend on from the others?
Lincoln borrowed the picture of a house from the Bible. Why is a house a good picture for a country? What did he think had to happen?
How might growing up in a small river town shape a person differently from working in a big city neighborhood? What might both places teach?

6.t: The First Peoples of North America
6.bq: How did the land shape the first peoples of North America, and how did meeting Europeans change both worlds?
std: Explain historical contexts and why groups in the same period held different perspectives
Compare how people adapt to and modify their environment in different places
Explain likely causes and effects of events and developments in U.S. history
Judge how useful a historical source is by its maker, date, origin, audience and purpose
Find sources with multiple points of view to help answer essential questions
6.write: Pick one Native nation or region from this unit. Make a claim about the biggest way meeting Europeans changed that nation's life. Support it with evidence from the readings, sources and data in the unit.
rooms: The first peoples — cards, quiz and lab

ch.bq: How did the land shape the many different ways Native peoples lived across North America?
ch.talk: Cahokia had no writing. What kinds of things would you look for in the ground if you wanted to learn how its people lived?
ch.story: Market Day Under the Great Mound

l.look: What can this one stone tell us about the people who made it? What can it not tell us?
Which region would be easiest for growing corn? Which would be hardest? How might that change what people ate?
Why is planting the three crops together smarter than planting each in its own field?

l.t: Bison and Tipis on the Plains
l.look: What happened to the bison between 1870 and 1890? What would that have meant for people who depended on them?

l.t: Pueblos and Ditches of the Southwest
l.look: Why might people choose to build their homes high in a cliff instead of down by the fields?

s.t: Coast, Ice and a Great City

l.t: Cedar and Salmon on the Northwest Coast
l.look: Why did people here have time to carve, build and hold big feasts when Plains peoples had to keep moving?

l.t: Ice and Sea in the Arctic
l.look: Count the animals this hunter depends on just to stand there. What would happen to his family if the seals disappeared?
Every basket of dirt in Monks Mound was carried by a person. What does that tell you about how Cahokia's people were organized?
What does it mean for a leader to have skin seven spans thick? Why would a council want leaders like that?
Brackenridge saw the mounds but not the people. What clues did he use to guess that a large city had stood there?
What in this scene is old, and what is new? Why is it a mistake to think of Native people only as part of the past?

ch.bq: When Europeans and Native peoples met, what changed for each of them, and who got to tell the story?
ch.talk: Pierre and Chicagou both walked away happy. What might each of them lose in the years ahead that they could not see on that day?
ch.story: Furs and Kettles on the River

l.look: If you could sail straight from Europe to India and skip all those middle steps, what would happen to the price? Who would gain and who would lose?
Columbus praised the Taíno and, in the same breath, planned to rule them. What does this tell you about how he saw them?

l.t: Corn Goes East, Wheat Goes West
l.look: Pick one food you ate this week. Was it from the Americas, from the rest of the world, or a mix? Could you have eaten it in 1491 where you live?
About how long did it take horses to travel from Mexico to the northern Plains? How did they get there without Spanish riders?
How could a disease reach a village before any European did? What would this do to a nation's ability to defend its land?
Why did Popé use knotted cords instead of a written message? What problems did he solve by having every pueblo act on the same day?
This is the French side of the meeting. What might an Illinois elder have written about the same day, if he had kept a journal?
Put the three countries in order of who arrived first in what is now the United States. Which reached Illinois?

s.t: Loss, Resistance and Points of View

l.look: Black Hawk was defeated, yet he was asked to tell his story and it was printed. Why might it matter that his side was written down at all?
Why might a language matter so much to a nation? How is learning it again a kind of resistance?
Both think they won. Is one of them wrong? What could a historian learn by reading both accounts instead of one?

7.bq: The founders promised liberty and equality. Who got it, who was left out, and how did the promise get stretched?
std: Explain likely causes and effects of events and developments in U.S. history
Build and use a timeline of related events to compare developments of the same period
SS.CV.2.5
Examine where rules, laws and key U.S. constitutional provisions come from and why
SS.CV.3.5
Compare the origins, functions and structure of different systems of government
Explain historical contexts and why groups in the same period held different perspectives
Investigate how the cultural and environmental characteristics of U.S. places change over time
7.write: The Declaration says all men are created equal. Make a claim: in the years from 1740 to 1840, did the United States keep that promise, break it, or do both? Use at least three pieces of evidence from this unit.
rooms: Explorers, colonies, a new nation — cards, quiz and lab

ch.bq: How did land, work and law shape life in the thirteen colonies, and who was free?
ch.talk: Anna and Cato both work hard. What is the biggest difference between their mornings? Why does it matter?

l.t: New England: Rocky Soil, Busy Harbors
l.look: What does the stone wall tell you about farming in New England? Why might a son from this farm choose to become a sailor?
Which region had two of the three biggest cities? What about that region might explain it?
Match each product to its region. How does the land explain the product?
Trace one sack of wheat from the wagon to a ship. Who touches it along the way?
How do these jobs compare to what you do at your age? What would be hardest?
What does this schoolbook tell you about what colonists thought school was for?
Why might he sign? What risks is he taking? How is his deal different from what happened to Cato's grandmother?
Why is a first-person account like this so important for understanding history? What can it tell us that a ship's record cannot?
Who got to raise a hand in this meeting? Who did not? Whose voice was missing?
If a ship took six weeks to reach London, how long would it take to ask a question and get an answer? What does that mean for who really made decisions?

ch.bq: Why did the colonies break from Britain, and what kind of government did they build instead?
ch.talk: Why do you think the delegates kept the windows shut and the doors guarded? What are the good and bad sides of making a big decision in secret?

l.look: What exactly are the colonists claiming? Are they asking to leave Britain, or something else?
Which picture would you trust more, and why? What does each side want you to believe?
How many years passed from the first big tax to the first shots? Did the fight speed up or slow down near the end?
Self-evident means obvious without proof. Was equality obvious in 1776? Who in the colonies would have said no?
About what fraction of the army died that winter without a single battle? Why would soldiers stay?
Why did the French navy matter so much? What would have happened at Yorktown without it?
Which of these numbers caused the most trouble? Why would a government with no taxes fail?
It starts with We the People, not We the States. Why does that choice matter?
Count the freedoms in this one sentence. Which one would the Boston Tea Party protesters have cared about most?
Which state gets more seats in Congress? Who gains from that, and who does not?
How many years passed between the Bill of Rights and women winning the vote? What does that tell you about how change happens?

ch.bq: How did the United States grow so fast, and who paid the price for that growth?
ch.talk: Sarah's family gave up everything they knew for eighty acres of prairie. What would make a family take that risk? Who lived on that land before them?

s.t: First Steps of a New Nation

l.look: Which of Washington's warnings do you think Americans followed? Which did they ignore?
Why might Napoleon sell so much land so cheaply? What did the United States gain besides land?
Why did Jefferson want notebooks and drawings, not just a report that they arrived? Who helped make the journey possible?
Why would a national law about land say something about schools? What does the second sentence mean for a family like Sarah's, floating past Kentucky?
About how many times bigger was Illinois in 1850 than in 1820? Where do you think those people came from?
Why was going upstream such a big deal? What new things could a farmer do once boats went both ways?
If Chicago is about 300 miles from St. Louis, about how many hours would each take? Why did railroads win?
The Cherokee used the law, the courts and petitions. Why did none of it work? What does that tell you about power?
The gin made cleaning fifty times faster. Why did that make planters want more enslaved workers, not fewer?

l.t: A Bigger Country, a Bigger Argument
l.look: Why would a line on a map calm the argument for a while? Why could it not settle the argument for good?

8.bq: Who holds the power in a democracy, and what does each person owe to the community in return?
std: SS.CV.1.4
Distinguish the powers and responsibilities of local, state and national government officials
SS.CV.2.4
Explain how democracy depends on responsible participation and how individuals should take part
SS.CV.3.4
Identify civic virtues and democratic principles that guide Illinois and the nation
SS.CV.4.4
Explain how rules and laws change society and how people change laws in Illinois
SS.CV.4.5
Explain how policies are developed to address public problems
Identify local problems and some of the ways people are working to address them
8.write: Make a claim: Is voting or speaking up the more powerful tool for changing a community? Use evidence from the stop sign story, the crosswalk story, and the lives of Jane Addams or Ida B. Wells to support your claim.
rooms: Government: local, state, national — cards, quiz and lab

ch.t: What Government Does and Who Decides
ch.bq: Who decides the rules for a town, a state and a country, and how do they decide?
ch.talk: Mr. Kowalski lost the vote. Was the meeting still fair to him? Why or why not?
ch.story: The Stop Sign on Maple Street

l.look: Count the things in Maya's day that a government paid for or made a rule about. Which one matters most to you?
Why might a problem in Springfield be easier for a local government to fix than for the national government?
Sort the five jobs into local, state and national. Which one was hardest to place, and why?
The first three words are "We the People." Who does that say the government belongs to?
If you sat on the council, how would you split the money? Who might be unhappy with your choice?
Why do you think a state has more than one hundred lawmakers but only one governor?
Illinois has seventeen members in the House but only two senators. Why does a small state like Wyoming also get two senators?

l.t: From an Idea to a Law
l.look: The House has 118 members and the Senate has 59. Three out of five are needed to beat a veto. Does the recess bill become a law? Show your math.
A U.S. Representative must run again every two years. A senator waits six. How might that change how each one acts?
Lincoln uses the word "people" three times. What is different about "of," "by" and "for"?
Which plan helps the most students? Which plan helps people outside the school? How would you vote, and what would you say to the rooms that lost?

ch.bq: What does a citizen get from the government, what does a citizen owe, and how can one person make things fairer?
ch.talk: Which of the eight steps do you think mattered most? What would have happened if the four had skipped the car count?

l.look: Why might it be more important to list what a leader cannot do than what a student cannot do?
Find the five freedoms in this one sentence. Which one did the four friends use to get their crosswalk?
The word "impartial" means not taking sides. Why would it be unfair if a jury already took one side before the trial started?
If your town had to cut one thing from that list, which would hurt the most people? Which would hurt the fewest?

l.t: Serving on a Jury and Voting
l.look: Mr. Okafor did not want to go. Why is it important that people like him, and not only judges, decide cases?
Which message is more likely to get the swing fixed? What does Message B have that Message A does not?
Pick one goal from this list. How did the crosswalk story help meet that goal?
What would you propose, and what would you write to your state representative to convince them?
Which of these numbers would matter most to a council member worried about safety? Which would matter most to one worried about money?
Which of these three jobs could a government have done? Which one might a government have done worse than the volunteers?
Addams said she needed her neighbors as much as they needed her. What might she have meant?

l.t: Ida B. Wells Tells the Truth
l.look: Wells fought with numbers and names instead of weapons. Why can facts be so powerful against injustice?

9.bq: How do scarce resources and the shape of the land decide what people make, trade and do where they live?
std: SS.EC.1.5
Analyze why and how individuals, businesses and nations specialize and trade
SS.EC.2.4
Describe how goods and services are made using human, natural and capital resources
SS.EC.3.5
Determine how government pays for the goods and services it provides
Describe how people have used natural resources across the United States
Investigate how the cultural and environmental characteristics of U.S. places change over time
9.write: Make a claim: Is Illinois a better place for a farm or for a big city? Use evidence from both chapters, such as the soil, the rivers, the climate, Chicago's railroads and what prices and trade do, to support your claim.
rooms: Money, markets and choices — cards, quiz and lab
Maps and regions of the United States — cards, quiz and lab

ch.bq: Why can't we have everything we want, and how do people decide what to make, buy and share?
ch.talk: Was raising the price fair? What else could the class have done so that every kid got a pencil?
ch.story: The Day the Pencils Ran Out

l.look: List each moment when Mr. Kim is a producer and each moment when he is a consumer.
Sort each thing the family paid for into goods or services. Which list is longer?

l.t: Scarcity and the Choice You Give Up
l.look: What was the opportunity cost of Jalen's choice? Why can it only be one thing, not two?
What changed demand between the first two days? What changed it on the third day?
What is happening to demand and supply? What could the owner do, and who would be helped or hurt?
Benevolence means kindness. Smith says the baker bakes for his own reasons, not just to be nice. How does that still end up feeding you?
If the bike costs one hundred dollars, about how many weeks will Amara need? What could she change to get there sooner?
What does Ms. Lopez gain by borrowing? What does she risk? Where does the bank get the money to lend her?
What two reasons does the Constitution give for collecting taxes? Name one public good that fits each reason.
Orange trees die when it stays below freezing (32 degrees) for long. Use the numbers to explain why Florida, not Illinois, grows oranges.

l.t: Why Trade Makes Both Sides Better
l.look: What should each farm grow? What should they do next? Would they have more or less if each tried to grow both?
What need did Tasha spot? What is her risk? What would you tell her to find out before she starts?

ch.bq: How do the land, water and weather of a place shape how people there live and work?
ch.talk: Why does corn from the middle of the country travel by river instead of by truck the whole way? What would change if the river were not there?

l.look: Which city on the list is closest to the equator? Which two Illinois cities are near each other? What would you guess about their winters?
About how many real miles is Springfield from Chicago? About how far is Cairo? Which drive would take longer?
Which sides of Illinois probably follow rivers? Which sides did people draw with a ruler? How could a physical map help you check?
About how many times bigger is New York City than Chicago? Which region's largest city is the smallest on this list?
How does the Southeast's climate change what a farmer can grow and when? What crops could the Illinois farmer grow that the Georgia farmer might not?
Which region has the tallest mountain? About how many times taller is Mount Whitney than the highest point in Illinois?
Bates wrote this after a train trip across the country. Which region do amber waves of grain describe? Which region has purple mountains?
Which of these rivers lies entirely inside Illinois? Why do you think early towns like Peoria and Cairo grew on rivers?

l.t: Jobs and Food From the Land
l.look: Match each job to its place. What natural resource makes each job possible there and not somewhere else?
Twain was a riverboat pilot before he was a writer. Why might a river have seemed like the most important road in the country in the 1800s?
Name the hazard in each place. Which one gives the most warning? Which gives the least? How does that change how people prepare?

10.bq: What did people gain and lose when they moved from hunting and gathering to farming, cities and states?
std: Classify historical events and developments as examples of change or continuity
Classify the kinds of historical sources used in secondary interpretations
SS.H.3.6-8.MdC
Detect possible gaps in the historical record from different kinds of sources
Explain how humans and their environment affect one another
Explain multiple causes and effects of historical events
10.write: Was the shift from hunting and gathering to farming and cities a good deal for the people who lived through it? Make a claim, support it with at least three pieces of evidence from this unit, and explain your reasoning.
rooms: The world before 1500 — cards, quiz and lab

ch.bq: Why did people who had hunted and gathered for tens of thousands of years start to farm, and what did that choice cost them?
ch.talk: The cousins gained a full storehouse and a permanent home. What do you think they gave up? Would you have stayed or walked on?
ch.story: The Autumn Some of Them Stayed

l.look: What can you say for certain about the people who camped here? What would you only be guessing?
About how many years passed between the Chauvet paintings and the first writing? What does that gap tell you about how much of the human story is prehistory?
Why would people go to so much trouble to paint in a place that was dark, cold and hard to reach? What does the location itself suggest?
Which food was more dependable? Why might a band that shared everything do better than one where each family kept what it found?
